title: Using CycleGANs to Generate Realistic STEM Images for Machine Learning and Atom-By-Atom Analysis on the Million-Atom Scale
content: Our work presents a novel approach for generating large amounts of realistic, labeled training data for machine learning (ML) applications using a cycle generative adversarial network (CycleGAN). ML techniques are catalyzing an era of data-driven materials research, enabling new possibilities such as autonomous collection and processing of massive, atomic resolution electron microscopy data sets on the scale of millions or even hundreds of millions of atoms. However, developing ML models that can reliably handle new or changing experimental conditions in such large data sets remains challenging. Here, we address this challenge by developing a CycleGAN with a novel reciprocal space discriminator, which learns the complicated, low and high spatial frequency information from experimental data and transfers this information to simulated images. We demonstrate that this CycleGAN can convert easily-generated, but unrealistic, simulated data into realistic images that are nearly indistinguishable from experiment (Figure 1). Such images are valuable because they represent a new method to rapidly generate labeled, experimentally realistic training data for ML-based image analysis—thereby addressing a major barrier that has previously limited the accuracy, ease-of-use, and generalizability of ML in materials characterization. We demonstrate the usefulness of these CycleGAN-processed images by training a fully convolutional network (FCN) to identify single atom defects in a large, automatically acquired data set with 4.5 million atoms using an aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM). Notably, we find that the CycleGAN can perform well even when trained with only 6 experimental images. This opens the door to dynamically evolving ML models, which can adapt to changing experiment or sample conditions. These results [1,2] represent an important step towards autonomous, large-scale data collection and processing of materials characterization data [3].
